tagline: Stories of faithful exiles in a pagan court and visions of beastly empires, both declaring that the Most High rules and that God's kingdom will outlast them all.
overview:
Daniel is two books in one cover. The first six chapters are court stories: a young man from Judah and his three friends, carried off to Babylon, are trained for the king's service and survive a series of crises. They refuse the king's food, interpret dreams no one else can read, walk out of a furnace, watch a proud king lose his mind and a drunken king lose his kingdom, and come up alive from a den of lions. The last six chapters are visions, told by Daniel in the first person, in which beasts rise from the sea, horns grow and break, angels explain what the prophet cannot grasp, and history marches toward a time of terrible persecution and then an end in which God's people receive the kingdom.

One conviction holds the halves together. Nebuchadnezzar learns it the hard way: "the Most High rules over the kingdom of mankind and gives it to whom He wishes" (4:25). Empires are real and they are dangerous, but they are temporary, and they answer to a throne higher than their own. The stories show how to live faithfully inside such an empire, serving it honestly while refusing to worship it. The visions show where the empires are going and promise that suffering saints will not be forgotten.

The book matters far beyond its size. It gave Jewish and Christian readers the language of apocalyptic hope, including the clearest Old Testament statement of bodily resurrection (12:2). It gave Jesus the title he used for himself more than any other, the Son of Man, drawn from the figure who comes with the clouds of heaven in chapter 7. And it has sustained believers under hostile governments in every century since, from the Maccabean martyrs to Christians under modern persecution.
author:
The book never names its author outright. Chapters 1 to 6 speak of Daniel in the third person, while chapters 7 to 12 are largely his own first-person account ("I, Daniel"), and Jewish and Christian tradition has taken Daniel himself as the source of the whole. Jesus refers to "the prophet Daniel" (Matthew 24:15), and most Christians through the centuries have read the book as the work of the sixth-century exile it describes.

Most modern critical scholars hold that the book reached its final form from an unknown author or circle of pious Jews (sometimes linked with the wise teachers of 11:33 and 12:3) during the persecution under Antiochus IV in the 160s BC. On that view the court stories are older traditions, perhaps from the Persian or early Greek period, and the visions were written for readers suffering under Antiochus, set in the mouth of a famous figure from the past, a practice common in Jewish apocalyptic writing of the period. Others hold a mediating view: that a historical Daniel stands behind the stories and some of the visions, but that the material was gathered, edited, and extended in later centuries.

Ezekiel names a righteous and wise Daniel alongside Noah and Job (Ezekiel 14:14, 20; 28:3). Some identify him with the Daniel of this book; others note that the spelling differs slightly and think Ezekiel means an ancient figure of legend, possibly the Danel known from texts found at Ugarit.
date:
The date of Daniel is one of the most debated questions in Old Testament study, and the debate is really about how the visions work.

The traditional view places the book in the sixth century BC, written by or from Daniel, who lived from the first deportation (about 605 BC) into the reign of Cyrus (after 539 BC). Its defenders point to the book's own claims, to Jesus' reference to Daniel as a prophet, to the book's knowledge of sixth-century details (such as Belshazzar, whose existence and role as co-regent were long doubted and are now confirmed by Babylonian texts), and to the conviction that God can reveal the future. They also note that copies of Daniel were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls, the oldest from the late second century BC, which leaves little time for a book written in the 160s to be copied and treated as Scripture.

The critical view dates the book, in its final form, to about 167 to 164 BC. Its defenders argue that chapter 11 traces the wars of the Ptolemies and Seleucids in precise detail down to the persecution of Antiochus IV, then becomes vague and does not match what happened at his death in 164 BC, which suggests a writer living just before that death. They add that the book's Aramaic and some loanwords (including Greek names for musical instruments in chapter 3) fit a later date, that some details of the sixth-century setting are puzzling (such as Darius the Mede), and that the Hebrew Bible places Daniel among the Writings rather than the Prophets. An old version of this argument goes back to the pagan philosopher Porphyry in the third century AD, whom Jerome answered in his commentary on Daniel.

Mediating positions hold that the stories and some visions come from the exile or the Persian period and that the book was completed later. Readers who share a firm confession about God's rule and Scripture's authority differ on this question.
setting:
The stories are set in the royal courts of Babylon and Persia. Nebuchadnezzar II (605 to 562 BC) made Babylon the dominant power of the Near East, defeating Egypt at Carchemish in 605 BC, taking captives from Judah that year (by Daniel's account, 1:1-3) and again in 597 BC, and destroying Jerusalem and its temple in 587 or 586 BC. After his death the empire weakened. Its last king, Nabonidus, spent about ten years at the oasis of Tema in Arabia and left his son Belshazzar in charge at Babylon. In 539 BC Babylon fell to Cyrus the Persian, whose empire would rule the region for two centuries until Alexander the Great conquered it in the 330s BC.

The visions look further ahead, to the kingdoms that would follow Babylon and above all to the Greek period. After Alexander's death in 323 BC his empire split among his generals. Two of their dynasties, the Ptolemies in Egypt and the Seleucids in Syria, fought over Judea for more than a century. In 167 BC the Seleucid king Antiochus IV Epiphanes banned Jewish worship, set up a pagan altar in the Jerusalem temple, and put faithful Jews to death. The revolt led by Judas Maccabeus retook and rededicated the temple in 164 BC, the event remembered at Hanukkah. On either view of the date, these events stand behind chapters 8 and 11, and the book's first readers under Antiochus found in it both a warning and a promise.
purpose: Daniel was written to strengthen God's people when they had no political power and every reason to think their God had lost. The stories model a faith that can serve a foreign empire with excellence and still refuse to bow to its gods, and they show God able to protect his servants or to be trusted even if he does not (3:17-18). The visions put persecution inside a larger frame: the beasts have their time, their time is measured, the heavenly court sits, and the kingdom is finally given to the saints of the Most High. The book calls for endurance and wisdom rather than panic, and it holds out resurrection as the answer to martyrdom (12:2-3). Its readers were exiles in Babylon, Jews under Persian and Greek rule, and the Maccabean generation facing death for their faith, and the book has spoken to every community in a similar place since.
story: Daniel sits in the exile, the great crisis of the Old Testament. Kings and Chronicles tell how Judah fell; Jeremiah and Ezekiel explain why; Ezra, Nehemiah, and Esther tell of the return and of life under Persia. Daniel covers the whole period of Babylonian captivity, from the first deportation (1:1) to the first year of Cyrus (1:21), and then looks beyond it to centuries of rule by foreign empires. It answers a question the exile raised: if the house of David has fallen and the temple is gone, is God still king? Daniel's answer is yes, and it widens Israel's hope from a return to the land to a kingdom that fills the whole earth (2:35) and a resurrection beyond death. That wider hope is the one the New Testament picks up.
christ:
Daniel shaped the vocabulary of the Gospels. Jesus announced that "the kingdom of God is near" (Mark 1:15), and Daniel is the Old Testament book most concerned with the kingdom that God himself sets up (2:44; 7:14, 27). Jesus called himself the Son of Man more than by any other title, and at his trial he joined Psalm 110 to Daniel 7:13, telling the high priest that he would see "the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power and coming with the clouds of heaven" (Mark 14:62). He spoke of "the abomination of desolation" described by Daniel (Matthew 24:15). Revelation borrows Daniel's beasts and its description of the Ancient of Days for the risen Christ (Revelation 1:13-14; 13:1-2).

The stories also carry a pattern the gospel completes: a faithful servant condemned by the powers, placed in a sealed pit, and brought out alive, with a pagan ruler then confessing God's kingdom (chapter 6). That likeness is a pattern, not a prediction, but the early church saw it clearly. Daniel's hope of resurrection (12:2) and of a kingdom given to a human figure from the presence of God find their fulfillment, in Christian confession, in the risen Jesus.
reading:
Read Daniel as two kinds of writing. The court stories are narratives with the shape of tales about wise courtiers: a crisis, a failure of the pagan experts, the rise of the Jewish hero, and a king who praises God. The visions are apocalyptic, a genre in which a seer receives revelation through dreams and symbolic images (beasts, horns, numbers), usually with an angel as interpreter, and in which history is shown from heaven's side and moving toward God's final judgment. Apocalyptic symbols are not code to be cracked line by line against the news. They are pictures meant to show what powers are like and who finally rules them, and Daniel often supplies its own interpretation.

Notice that the book is written in two languages. Daniel 1:1 to 2:4a and chapters 8 to 12 are in Hebrew; 2:4b to 7:28 is in Aramaic, the common language of the empires. The switch does not match the division between stories and visions, so chapters 2 to 7 form their own unit. Chapters 2 and 7 both describe four kingdoms followed by God's kingdom, and they frame the Aramaic section.

The four kingdoms are read in two main ways. The older view, found in Jerome and held by most Christian interpreters until modern times and by many today, identifies them as Babylon, Media-Persia, Greece, and Rome. The other view, held by most critical scholars and some others, identifies them as Babylon, Media, Persia, and Greece, with the fourth beast's little horn as Antiochus IV. Futurist readers add that the fourth kingdom, or its final stage, reaches into the end of history. The Greek versions of Daniel include further stories (Susanna, Bel and the Dragon, and the Prayer of Azariah with the Song of the Three Young Men), which Roman Catholic and Orthodox Bibles include and Protestant Bibles place in the Apocrypha.

structure.title: Faithful in Babylon
structure.summary: Daniel and his three friends are taken into the king's service, refuse the royal food, and are given wisdom by God. The chapter, in Hebrew, introduces the characters and the setting of the whole book.

structure.title: The Aramaic chapters: kingdoms and the kingdom of God
structure.summary: Stories of dreams, a furnace, a humbled king, writing on a wall, and a lions' den, framed by two visions of four kingdoms (chapters 2 and 7). Chapter 7 begins the visions but belongs to this Aramaic unit.

structure.title: The ram and the goat
structure.summary: The book returns to Hebrew with a vision of Persia and Greece and a little horn that attacks the sanctuary, widely identified with Antiochus IV.

structure.title: Daniel's prayer and the seventy weeks
structure.summary: Reading Jeremiah's seventy years, Daniel confesses Israel's sin, and Gabriel answers with a prophecy of seventy weeks of years.

structure.title: The final vision
structure.summary: A long revelation of wars between the kings of the north and south, the persecution of the faithful, and the promise of resurrection at the end.

themes.title: The Most High rules
themes.body: Every chapter presses the same claim: God gives kingdoms and takes them away. Nebuchadnezzar is made to confess it (4:34-37), Belshazzar ignores it and dies (chapter 5), and Darius decrees it (6:26). The visions show the same truth on a larger canvas. Empires rise like beasts from a churning sea, but a court sits in heaven and their dominion is taken away.

themes.title: Faithfulness in exile
themes.body: Daniel and his friends learn Babylon's language and literature, take Babylonian names, and serve its kings with integrity. They draw the line at worship and at what would defile them. The book offers a model for living as a minority under a power that does not share your faith: neither withdrawal nor surrender, but loyal service with a limit.

themes.title: Wisdom that comes from God
themes.body: The wise men of Babylon, with their omens and dream manuals, fail again and again. Daniel succeeds not because he is cleverer but because God "reveals the deep and hidden things" (2:22). Wisdom in Daniel is both learning and revelation, and in the later chapters it is the calling of the wise to understand the times and to lead many to righteousness.

themes.title: Suffering, endurance, and resurrection
themes.body: The visions are honest about persecution: the saints are handed over for a time, the sanctuary is trampled, and the wise fall by sword and flame. Deliverance does not always come before death. The book's final answer is resurrection, the dead awakening to everlasting life or disgrace, and the promise that the faithful will shine like the stars (12:2-3).

themes.title: The kingdom given to the Son of Man
themes.body: Human empires are pictured as beasts; God's kingdom is given to one like a son of man, a human figure who comes with the clouds and receives everlasting dominion, and it is shared with the saints of the Most High (7:13-14, 27). The New Testament hears this as the heart of Jesus' own claim.

keyChapters.why: Nebuchadnezzar's statue dream sets out four kingdoms followed by a stone that becomes a mountain and fills the earth, the kingdom God himself establishes.
Three young men refuse to worship the golden statue and are delivered in the furnace, the book's classic picture of faith that will not bow.
Nebuchadnezzar's madness and restoration, told in his own voice, teach that the Most High rules the kingdoms of men and humbles the proud.
Daniel keeps praying despite the king's decree and is delivered from the lions, a story of quiet, costly faithfulness.
The vision of four beasts and the Ancient of Days, where one like the Son of Man receives an everlasting kingdom, the source of Jesus' favorite title for himself.
Daniel's prayer of confession and the prophecy of seventy weeks, one of the most debated passages in the Bible.
The book closes with the clearest Old Testament promise of the resurrection of the dead.

parts.body:
Daniel is two books in one cover. The first six chapters are stories. A young man from Judah named Daniel and his three friends are carried off to Babylon and trained to serve its king. They refuse the king's food, explain dreams no one else can read, walk out of a blazing furnace, watch a proud king lose his mind and a drunken king lose his kingdom, and come up alive from a den of lions.

The last six chapters are visions, told by Daniel himself. Beasts rise from the sea, horns grow and break, angels explain what Daniel cannot grasp, and history moves toward a time of terrible persecution and then an end in which God's people receive the kingdom.

One conviction holds the two halves together. A king learns it the hard way: ‘the Most High rules over the kingdom of mankind and gives it to whom He wishes’ (4:17). Empires are real and they are dangerous, but they do not last, and they answer to a throne above their own. The stories show how to live faithfully inside such an empire, serving it honestly while refusing to worship it. The visions show where the empires are going, and promise that God's suffering people will not be forgotten.

The book's reach is far greater than its size. It gave Jewish and Christian readers the language of hope beyond death, including the clearest Old Testament statement that the dead will rise (12:2). It gave Jesus the title he used for himself more than any other, the Son of Man, from the figure who comes with the clouds of heaven in chapter 7. And it has strengthened believers under hostile rulers in every century since.

parts.h: Where it sits in the story
parts.body:
Daniel belongs to the exile, the great crisis of the Old Testament. The books of Kings and Chronicles tell how Judah fell. Jeremiah and Ezekiel explain why. Ezra, Nehemiah and Esther tell of the return and of life under Persia. Daniel covers the whole time of the Babylonian captivity, from the first deportation (1:1) to the first year of King Cyrus (1:21), and then looks far beyond it, to centuries of rule by foreign empires.

It answers a question the exile raised. If the house of David has fallen and the temple is gone, is God still king? Daniel's answer is yes. And it widens Israel's hope, from a return to the land to a kingdom that fills the whole earth (2:35), and to a resurrection beyond death (12:2).

In the Hebrew Bible, Daniel stands among the Writings, not among the Prophets. In English Bibles it stands with the prophets, after Ezekiel. Catholic and Orthodox Bibles also include further stories kept in Greek: the Prayer of Azariah and the Song of the Three Young Men in chapter 3, and the stories of Susanna and of Bel and the Dragon. Protestant Bibles place these in the Apocrypha.

The book does not name its author outright. Chapters 1 to 6 speak of Daniel in the third person. Chapters 7 to 12 are largely his own account, told in the first person. Jewish and Christian tradition took Daniel himself as the source of the whole, and Jesus speaks of ‘the prophet Daniel’ (Matthew 24:15).

The date of Daniel is one of the most debated questions in the study of the Old Testament, and the debate is really about how the visions work. These notes take no side, and set out each view as its holders state it.

The traditional view places the book in the sixth century BC, written by Daniel or from him, who lived from the first deportation, about 605 BC, into the reign of Cyrus after 539 BC. Its defenders, among them E. J. Young, Joyce Baldwin and Stephen Miller, point to the book's own claims, to Jesus' words, to details of the Babylonian and Persian court they regard as accurate, such as Belshazzar's place beside his father, and to the conviction that God can reveal the future. They also note that copies of Daniel were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls, at least one probably from the late second century BC.

The critical view, held by most modern critical scholars such as John J. Collins, dates the visions in their final form to about 167 to 164 BC, during the persecution under the Greek king Antiochus IV, with the court stories older. Its defenders argue that chapter 11 traces the wars of that age in close detail down to Antiochus's persecution, and then does not match what happened at his death. An old form of this argument goes back to the philosopher Porphyry in the third century AD, whom Jerome answered in his commentary on Daniel.

Mediating views hold that the stories and some visions come from the exile or the Persian period, and that the book was completed later. Readers who share a firm confession about God's rule and Scripture's authority differ on this question.

parts.h: Babylon, Persia, and the Greek kings
parts.body:
The stories are set in the courts of Babylon and Persia. Nebuchadnezzar II ruled Babylon from 605 to 562 BC. As crown prince he defeated Egypt at Carchemish in 605, and by Daniel's account took captives from Judah that year (1:1-3). More were taken in 597 BC, and Jerusalem and its temple were destroyed in 587 or 586 BC.

After Nebuchadnezzar the empire weakened. Its last king, Nabonidus (556 to 539 BC), spent about ten years at the oasis of Tayma in Arabia and left his son Belshazzar in charge at Babylon. That explains why Belshazzar could offer Daniel only the third place in the kingdom (5:29): he himself was second. In 539 BC Babylon fell to the Persian king Cyrus, almost without a fight. The ‘Darius the Mede’ who receives the kingdom in 5:31 is not known from other sources, and scholars have proposed several identifications.

The visions look further ahead. Alexander the Great conquered the Persian Empire between 334 and 331 BC and died at Babylon in 323. His generals divided his empire. Two of their families matter for Daniel: the Ptolemies, who ruled Egypt, and the Seleucids, who ruled Syria and Mesopotamia. Judea lay between them, and chapter 11 traces their wars as the struggles of ‘the king of the South’ and ‘the king of the North’.

The Seleucid king Antiochus IV Epiphanes (175 to 164 BC) tried to force Greek religion on Jerusalem. In 167 BC he desecrated the temple and banned Jewish worship, and faithful Jews were put to death. The revolt led by Judas Maccabeus retook and rededicated the temple in 164 BC, the event remembered at Hanukkah. On every view of the date, these events stand behind chapters 8 and 11.

Daniel is built of two kinds of writing. The court stories of chapters 1 to 6 have the shape of tales about wise courtiers: a crisis, the failure of the king's experts, the rise of the faithful Jew, and a king who ends by praising God. The visions of chapters 7 to 12 are apocalyptic writing. A seer receives revelation through dreams and symbolic pictures, usually with an angel to explain them, and history is shown from heaven's side, moving toward God's judgment.

The book is also written in two languages. It begins in Hebrew, switches to Aramaic at 2:4, when the king's wise men speak, stays in Aramaic through chapter 7, and returns to Hebrew for chapters 8 to 12. Aramaic was the common language of the empires. The switch does not match the line between stories and visions, so chapters 2 to 7 form a unit of their own. Chapters 2 and 7 both describe four kingdoms followed by God's kingdom, and they frame that unit.

This matters for reading. Apocalyptic symbols are not a code to be matched line by line against the news. They are pictures meant to show what powers are like and who finally rules them, and Daniel often gives its own interpretation. The angel says of the four beasts, ‘These four great beasts are four kings who will arise from the earth’ (7:17). Where the book interprets its own symbols, the reader should take its interpretation. Where it does not, the reader should be humble.

The stories show four young men living as a small minority under a power that does not share their faith. They learn Babylon's language and literature. They take Babylonian names. They serve its kings with integrity, and the king finds them ‘ten times better than all the magicians and enchanters in his entire kingdom’ (1:20). The book does not treat learning Babylon's wisdom as sin.

But they draw a line. Daniel will not defile himself with the king's food (1:8), and he asks permission rather than rebelling. Why he refused is debated: the food laws, food offered to idols, or the loyalty that eating from the king's table implied. The text does not settle it.

In chapter 3 the line is worship. Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego will not bow to the golden statue. Their answer to the king is one of the bravest sentences in the Bible. God is able to deliver them, they say, ‘But even if He does not, let it be known to you, O king, that we will not serve your gods or worship the golden statue you have set up’ (3:18). They are thrown into the furnace, and a fourth figure walks with them in the fire.

In chapter 6 the line is prayer. A decree forbids praying to anyone but the king for thirty days. Daniel goes home to his upper room, whose windows open toward Jerusalem, and prays three times a day ‘just as he had done before’ (6:10). He is thrown to the lions, and God shuts their mouths.

The pattern is neither withdrawal nor surrender. It is loyal service with a limit. And the stories do not promise that faith is always rescued. The friends' even if he does not is part of the lesson.

parts.h: Dreams, a humbled king, and writing on the wall
parts.body:
In chapter 2 Nebuchadnezzar dreams of a great statue with a head of gold, chest of silver, belly of bronze, legs of iron and feet of iron mixed with clay. A stone cut without hands strikes the feet, and the whole statue is broken and blown away, while the stone becomes a mountain that fills the earth. Daniel explains it: four kingdoms, and then ‘the God of heaven will set up a kingdom that will never be destroyed’ (2:44). His wisdom comes because God ‘reveals the deep and hidden things’ (2:22), not because he is cleverer than the king's experts.

In chapter 4 the king tells his own story. He dreams of a great tree cut down, and Daniel warns him to turn from his sins. A year later, walking on his palace roof and boasting of the Babylon he built, he loses his reason and lives like an animal in the fields until he acknowledges that the Most High rules. When his sanity returns, he praises God: ‘For His dominion is an everlasting dominion’ (4:34).

In chapter 5 Belshazzar holds a feast and drinks from the gold and silver vessels taken from the temple in Jerusalem. A hand appears and writes on the wall. Daniel reads the words, MENE, TEKEL and PERES, and explains them: God has numbered the days of his reign, he has been weighed and found wanting, and his kingdom is divided and given to the Medes and Persians (5:26-28). That night Belshazzar is killed.

The three stories teach the same thing in three ways. One king learns to confess God's rule. Another refuses and is removed. Pride is the danger the book names in its rulers.

parts.h: Four beasts, and one like a son of man
parts.body:
Chapter 7 is the hinge of the book. Daniel sees four beasts rise from a churning sea: a lion with eagle's wings, a bear, a leopard with four heads, and a fourth beast, terrifying, with iron teeth and ten horns. A little horn comes up among the horns and speaks boastful words.

Then the scene turns to heaven. Thrones are set in place, ‘and the Ancient of Days took His seat’ (7:9). The court is convened and the books are opened. The fourth beast is destroyed. And Daniel sees ‘One like the Son of Man coming with the clouds of heaven’ (7:13). He comes to the Ancient of Days and receives dominion, glory and an everlasting kingdom. The angel adds that ‘the saints of the Most High will receive the kingdom and possess it forever’ (7:18). The little horn will oppress them ‘for a time, and times, and half a time’ (7:25), and then the court will take his dominion away.

The four kingdoms are read in two main ways. The older Christian reading, found in Jerome and held by many conservative interpreters, takes them as Babylon, Medo-Persia, Greece and Rome, so that God's kingdom arrives in the Roman period with Christ. The critical reading takes them as Babylon, Media, Persia and Greece, with the little horn as Antiochus IV. Futurist readers add that the fourth kingdom, or its last stage, reaches into the end of history. These notes take no side.

Who is the one like a son of man? In the vision he is a human figure set against the beasts, given the kingdom from God's own presence. Many scholars, and many Jewish interpreters, read him as standing for a people, faithful Israel, since the kingdom is then given to the saints. Others take him as an angel, most likely Michael. The traditional Jewish and Christian reading takes him as an individual whose kingdom his people share: he comes with the clouds, as only God does. That reading appears early in Jewish writings, in 4 Ezra, in the Talmud's Messiah who comes with the clouds, and in Rashi. The readings are not wholly exclusive. The New Testament hears in this figure the heart of Jesus' own claim.

parts.h: The ram, the goat, and the little horn
parts.body:
Chapter 8, back in Hebrew, gives a second vision. A ram with two horns charges west, north and south, until a goat with one great horn comes from the west and shatters it. The great horn is broken and four horns grow in its place. From one of them a little horn grows great, takes away the daily sacrifice and throws down the sanctuary.

This time the book names the powers itself. ‘The two-horned ram that you saw represents the kings of Media and Persia. The shaggy goat represents the king of Greece, and the large horn between his eyes is the first king’ (8:20-21). Readers on every side take the first king as Alexander the Great, whose empire split into four, and most identify the little horn of this chapter with Antiochus IV, who desecrated the temple in 167 BC.

The vision leaves Daniel exhausted and sick for days (8:27). It is not good news to him. The book is honest that seeing what is coming can be a weight to carry.

parts.h: Daniel's prayer and the seventy weeks
parts.body:
Chapter 9 begins with Daniel reading Scripture. He understands from the word of the LORD to Jeremiah ‘that the desolation of Jerusalem would last seventy years’ (9:2). So he prays. His prayer is a long confession for his people's sin, in which he includes himself, and it rests its plea not on Israel's righteousness but on God's great compassion.

The angel Gabriel answers with a word about ‘Seventy weeks’ (9:24), or seventy sevens, usually read as seventy weeks of years. The prophecy speaks of the rebuilding of Jerusalem, of an anointed one who will be cut off, of a prince whose people will destroy the city and the sanctuary, and of ‘the abomination that causes desolation’ (9:27). The BSB writes the Messiah, the Prince. The Hebrew mashiach means anointed one, and who is meant is one of the questions in dispute.

These four verses have produced a very wide range of readings. Some calculate the weeks to the ministry and death of Christ. The dispensational reading places a gap between the sixty-ninth and seventieth weeks, so that the last week is still future. The critical reading ends the weeks with Antiochus, and identifies the anointed one who is cut off with the high priest Onias III, murdered about 171 BC. Each reading is held by careful interpreters. These notes take no side, and they calculate no date from these numbers.

The chapter's own weight falls on the prayer. Daniel does not begin with the timetable. He begins with confession, and the answer comes while he is still praying.

parts.h: The last vision, and the dead who will awake
parts.body:
Chapters 10 to 12 are one long vision. In chapter 10 a heavenly messenger appears to Daniel beside the Tigris and tells him that he was delayed by ‘the prince of the kingdom of Persia’ until Michael came to help (10:13). Behind the wars of nations, the book suggests, there is a conflict in the unseen world.

Chapter 11 traces the wars of the king of the North and the king of the South (11:5-15) in close detail, which readers on all sides connect with the Seleucids and the Ptolemies. It comes to a king who desecrates the temple fortress and sets up ‘the abomination of desolation’ (11:31). Under him, ‘the people who know their God will firmly resist him’ (11:32), and some of the wise will fall by sword and flame. From verse 36 the king ‘will exalt and magnify himself above every god’ (11:36). Many read these verses as Antiochus IV, and note that the end described does not match how he died; others read them as a future figure beyond Antiochus. These notes identify no one of the present day with this king.

Then chapter 12 opens with a promise. Michael will rise. There will be a time of distress like no other, but everyone whose name is written in the book will be delivered. ‘And many who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake, some to everlasting life, but others to shame and everlasting contempt’ (12:2). ‘Then the wise will shine like the brightness of the heavens’ (12:3).

The book ends with Daniel asking how long, and receiving no timetable he can use. He is told to go his way. ‘You will rest, and will arise to your inheritance at the end of the days’ (12:13).

parts.h: How the New Testament reads Daniel
parts.body:
Daniel shaped the language of the Gospels. Jesus called himself the Son of Man more than by any other title. At his trial, asked whether he was the Christ, he said that he was, and joined Psalm 110 to Daniel 7:13: ‘you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power and coming with the clouds of heaven’ (Mark 14:62).

Jesus also spoke of ‘the abomination of desolation,’ described by the prophet Daniel (Matthew 24:15), as he foretold the destruction of the temple. That shows that the early church read Daniel's visions as still open to further fulfillment, beyond what had happened under Antiochus.

The kingdom Jesus announced, ‘the kingdom of God is near’ (Mark 1:15), is the kingdom Daniel 2 and 7 promised God would set up. The letter to the Hebrews remembers people of faith who ‘shut the mouths of lions, quenched the raging fire’ (Hebrews 11:33-34). And Revelation borrows Daniel's beasts and its picture of the Ancient of Days, whose hair was like pure wool, to describe the risen Christ (Revelation 1:13-14; 13:1-2).

These notes draw no line from Daniel to Christ that the New Testament does not draw itself. The likeness some readers see between Daniel brought alive out of the sealed den and the empty tomb is a pattern the church has noticed, not a prediction the book makes.

Daniel is Israel's own Scripture, written for Jews in exile and under persecution, and its hope of the kingdom and the resurrection is theirs before it is anyone else's. Nothing in it is a reason to speak against the Jewish people, then or now.

Read the book as its first hearers heard it: as a message to people under pressure from empires, who needed to know that God, not the beast, rules history. Read the stories for what they show about living faithfully in a culture that does not share your faith: neither withdrawal nor surrender, but honest service with a line that will not be crossed.

Read the visions as pictures first. Let the book interpret its own symbols where it does, and look to the rest of the Old Testament for the others. Treat the numbers as symbols before anything else. A time, and times, and half a time is three and a half, half of seven: a time of trouble that is real but cut short and limited by God.

Be humble about identifications. The history of reading Daniel is full of confident readings that tied a beast or a horn to an emperor, a pope, a sultan or a modern ruler, and every generation of such readers has been followed by another. These notes name no person, nation or movement of the present day as any figure in Daniel, and they set no date for the end from its numbers. Jesus said that no one knows the day or the hour (Matthew 24:36), and every date set by calculation has passed.

Be careful about fear, too. The book was written to give endurance and hope to people who were suffering, not to frighten the comfortable or feed speculation. Its last words to Daniel are rest, and rising.

If you are suffering now, for your faith or for any other reason, you do not have to carry it alone. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

hard.line: The third year of Jehoiakim: how the date fits Jeremiah 25:1 and the Babylonian Chronicle.
Why did Daniel refuse the king's food? Three readings, and the text does not settle it.
A king orders all the wise men of Babylon put to death because they cannot tell his dream.
The four kingdoms of the statue, read two ways.
‘But even if He does not’: faith that does not depend on being rescued.
Nebuchadnezzar's madness: a judgment on one king's pride, never a reading of anyone's illness.
Darius the Mede, not known from other sources.
The accusers thrown to the lions with their wives and children.
The fourth beast and the little horn, read two ways, with no figure of the present day named.
Who is the one like a son of man?
The fierce king of chapter 8, most often identified with Antiochus IV.
The seventy weeks: several readings, and no date calculated from them.
The prince of Persia, and conflict in the unseen world.
The abomination of desolation, and the wise who fall by sword and flame.
The king who exalts himself: Antiochus, or a figure beyond him?
The dead will awake, some to everlasting life and some to shame.
1,290 days and 1,335 days: numbers that set no date.

words.line: The book's favorite name for God among the nations, the God who rules over the kingdom of mankind (4:17).
The word that runs through the book. Human kingdoms rise and fall; God's ‘will never be destroyed’ (2:44).
The people whose dynasty ruled Babylon, and in Daniel also a class of scholars and diviners (1:4; 2:2).
Daniel's Babylonian name. His Hebrew name spoke of God as judge; the new name was a claim of ownership (1:7).
The common language of the empires. Daniel is written in it from 2:4 to the end of chapter 7, and in Hebrew around it.
The words written on the wall: numbered, weighed, divided. The kingdom is given to the Medes and Persians (5:25-28).
God as the aged judge on the throne of fire, with books opened before him (7:9-10).
In Aramaic bar enash, a human being. One like a son of man receives the everlasting kingdom (7:13-14). Jesus' favorite title for himself.
The holy ones, God's people, who receive the kingdom after the beast is judged (7:18, 27).
A power that grows great, speaks against the Most High and oppresses the saints (7:8; 8:9). Its identification is debated.

words.word: Time, times and half a time
words.line: Three and a half, half of seven: a time of trouble that is real but cut short by God (7:25; 12:7).
Seventy sevens, usually read as weeks of years, in Gabriel's answer to Daniel's prayer (9:24). Read in several ways.
Something set up in the temple that defiles it and leaves it desolate (9:27; 11:31; 12:11). Jesus takes up the phrase in Matthew 24:15.
In Hebrew maskilim, those with insight who instruct many and lead many to righteousness (11:33; 12:3).
The great prince who stands watch over Daniel's people (10:13; 12:1).

timeline.what: Nebuchadnezzar, as crown prince, defeats Egypt at Carchemish and becomes king of Babylon. By Daniel's account, Daniel and his friends are taken that year (1:1-6).
Nebuchadnezzar II reigns over Babylon. The stories of chapters 1 to 4 are set in his court.
A larger deportation takes King Jehoiachin and many others to Babylon, among them the prophet Ezekiel.
Jerusalem and the temple are destroyed. The temple vessels Belshazzar later drinks from were carried to Babylon (5:2-3).
Nabonidus, Babylon's last king, spends about ten years at Tayma and leaves his son Belshazzar in charge at Babylon (chapter 5).
Babylon falls to Cyrus of Persia. In Daniel, Belshazzar is killed and ‘Darius the Mede’ receives the kingdom (5:30-31).
Daniel remains in service until then (1:21). His last vision is dated to Cyrus's third year (10:1).
Alexander the Great conquers the Persian Empire and dies at Babylon. His empire divides, as the goat's great horn is broken and four grow up (8:8, 21-22).
The Seleucid Antiochus III wins Judea from the Ptolemies at the battle of Panium. Chapter 11 traces the wars of the kings of the north and south.
Antiochus IV Epiphanes reigns. About 171 BC the high priest Onias III is murdered, whom the critical reading takes as the anointed one cut off (9:26).
Antiochus desecrates the temple and bans Jewish worship, recorded in 1 Maccabees 1:54. Many read 11:31 of this.
Judas Maccabeus retakes and rededicates the temple, remembered at Hanukkah. Antiochus dies the same year.
The critical view dates the visions in their final form here; the traditional view places the book in the sixth century BC. Readers differ.
The oldest copy of Daniel found among the Dead Sea Scrolls at Qumran probably comes from about this time.
At his trial Jesus joins Daniel 7:13 to Psalm 110 to speak of himself (Mark 14:62).
Jerome's commentary on Daniel answers Porphyry, who had argued that the visions were written under Antiochus.

places.name: Jerusalem
places.line: The city Nebuchadnezzar besieged (1:1). In Babylon, Daniel prayed with his windows open toward it (6:10), and grieved its desolation (9:2).
